entry.title: Anmeldung (Registering Address) in Berlin
entry.content:
Back to Berlin

Since there are no in-person classes during my final semester, I’ve moved back to Berlin. While Aachen is a small, beautiful, and practical city, Berlin just feels a bit more like home to me.

Just as you would register your residence in Korea, any change of address in Germany requires notifying the local authority. It is typically the most straightforward and initial administrative procedure you encounter here, yet if you aren’t fluent in German, it can feel like a massive wall. My German is still extremely rusty, but somehow, I’ve managed to get through all three of my Anmeldungen so far.

An-/Um-/Abmeldung

Anmeldung is similar to Korea’s address registration (전입신고) and applies when you move to Germany for the first time or relocate to a residence outside your previous municipal jurisdiction. You are required to register within 14 days. Ummeldung applies when you move to a new address within the same jurisdiction. Abmeldung applies when your new residence is located outside Germany—meaning you are leaving the country altogether. 1

Since I am registering a change of address from Aachen to Berlin, it falls under Anmeldung, not Ummeldung or Abmeldung. Back when I did my Anmeldung in Aachen, I was told that my records at the local citizen’s office (Bürgeramt) would automatically transfer from Berlin to Aachen. I assumed the same applied to the Immigration Office (Ausländeramt, Landesamt für Einwanderung, or Migrationsamt) and the Tax Office (Finanzamt). However, the Aachen Immigration Office required a one-time in-person visit to transfer and process my file, while the Berlin Tax Office demanded justification regarding my primary/secondary residence. While you certainly don’t need to file a separate departure notice with your previous local office, it definitely pays to check how the specific administrative authorities at both ends handle their procedures.

Documents

There are two required documents:

  1. Registration Form (Anmeldung bei der Meldebehörde)
  2. Landlord Confirmation Form (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung)

Registration Form

Use the Registration Form Template provided by the ServicePortal Berlin.

anmeldung_bei_der_meldebehoerde.pdf
Loading PDF…

Landlord Confirmation Form

If your landlord or real estate agency provided a document when you signed the lease, you can use that directly. When I registered in Aachen previously, I submitted the document prepared by the agency. If not, you can request them to fill out the Landlord Confirmation Sample Form provided by the ServicePortal Berlin.

mdb-f402544-20161102_wohnungsgeberbestaetigung.pdf
Loading PDF…

Booking a Termin

If your move-in date is fixed, booking a Termin (appointment) actually takes priority over the move itself or preparing documents. The first time I registered in Berlin, and again in Aachen, getting an appointment for this simple administrative task meant waiting anywhere from 3 weeks to two full months. If you’re already late, your best bet is refreshing the booking page whenever you think of it, or hunting early in the morning when new slots or cancellations are released. Or… you can just snag whatever appointment is left anywhere in the city and treat yourself to a little tour of the Berlin U-Bahn.

In stark contrast to my past struggles, I logged onto the booking page this time with zero expectations, only to secure an appointment effortlessly. I even got to pick the Bürgeramt closest to my apartment and my preferred time slot. This is unheard of in Berlin, leaving both me and the locals I told completely stunned.

Online Termin

You can select a nearby Bürgeramt and choose an available date and time slot from the List of Local Offices on the Wohnsitz page on the ServicePortal Berlin.

No Online Anmeldung

Despite having an eID-enabled card and a BundID account, online Anmeldung wasn’t an option. Non-EU citizens are strictly required to book an appointment and process the registration on-site in writing. Online Anmeldung is reserved exclusively for German and EU citizens.2

The Appointment

First Attempt (2026-10-02)

I walked into the Bürgeramt with full confidence, only to run headfirst into a bizarre situation. When I registered in Aachen, my Berlin address had been registered as a secondary residence (Nebenwohnung). This was precisely why the Berlin Tax Office had previously demanded an explanation. Since Berlin is one of the cities that taxes secondary residences, you must avoid being registered with a Nebenwohnung when relocating to another city if you no longer live there or maintain the address.

Since I had brought my binder full of administrative records and documents (expats jokingly say the very first thing you must do upon arriving in Germany is buy a binder to collect paperwork), I quickly flipped through my Aachen Anmeldung files. Fortunately, my original application form was right there, where I had correctly listed my new Aachen address as my sole (einzige) residence and marked my Berlin address as deregistered (abgemeldet). Lacking the confidence to explain the situation in German, I asked if I could briefly explain my situation in English, only to receive a prompt, blunt “No.”

Eventually, an English-speaking employee nearby stepped in to help, took a look at the system, and broke the news:

“You have registered your address in Berlin as Nebenwohnung on [date] November last year.”

“Well.. no. That was not my intention. Could you please have a look at my applica…[tion form here]?”

Cutting me off mid-sentence, the reply came: “There is no ‘No’. That’s what we have on the system.”

To be fair, the civil servants I’ve encountered so far have been friendly enough (by German standards). I’m even grateful they don’t kick you out for not bringing a German translator like they used to. However, when a problem arises, I’ve noticed a recurring pattern: instead of offering potential solutions as experts who know the administrative process (not that I expect them to solve it for me…), they resort to a completely defensive posture.

And just like that, I walked out with nothing solved and the absurd response that there was nothing they could do in Berlin, suggesting I go all the way to the Aachen Bürgeramt in person to talk it out.

HW/NW

There is a difference between the document requiring your signature (retained by the authority) and the confirmation document issued to you after processing. I don’t recall the exact layout of the Aachen form, but the issued document contained no information about a secondary residence at all—despite the official’s misprocessing that kept my Berlin address as a Nebenwohnung! (Presumably, addresses outside their jurisdiction simply aren’t displayed.) It listed only “Hauptwohnung” (Since there was no annotation column like in Berlin, it should have been einzige or alleinige. Back then, I didn’t quite grasp the semantic nuance between einzige and Hauptwohnung.) On the form requiring a signature in Berlin, previous and future address statuses—whether sole, primary, or secondary, and whether maintained or deregistered—are explicitly marked for both locations. Conversely, the document I received simply stated “HW,” with a footnote reading “HW = Alleinige oder Hauptwohnung” (HW = Sole or Primary Residence).

Long story short, since things can be processed entirely contrary to your intentions depending on the official’s “Kibun” (mood/caprice), it’s best to keep a copy of your completed application or store it carefully if they return it to you (which is also completely random…).

Data Processing (2026-10-12)

Fortunately, the city of Aachen helped me resolve the error via email very quickly without requiring a personal visit. If you ever run into similar trouble, as the data subject, you can cite Sections 63 and 124 of the German Federal Act on Registration (Bundesmeldegesetz) regarding your right to data self-determination, accuracy, and completeness.

I booked another Termin (slots were surprisingly still plentiful!) and visited the Bürgeramt after the weekend, only to be told that the system hadn’t updated yet and to come back after waiting another week.

Done (2026-10-19)

For the first time, no appointments were available at my local neighborhood Bürgeramt, so I grabbed a single remaining or canceled slot at the adjacent office and visited. A civil servant with a thoroughly businesslike expression finally handed over the stamped Anmeldung document. It took about three weeks in total.

Survey

When booking a Termin, the city of Berlin asks whether you’d like to participate in a follow-up survey. I used to opt out every time out of laziness, but a German friend once told me a story that they only ever encountered friendly officials on the rare occasions they opted in…

Footnotes

  1. Bundesmeldegesetz (BMG) § 17 Registration, Deregistration, Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection ↩

  2. “Sie sind volljährig und besitzen die deutsche Staatsbürgerschaft oder sind EU-Bürger/in und Sie sind innerhalb Deutschlands umgezogen,” Residence - Register sole or main residence, ServicePortal Berlin ↩

  3. Bundesmeldegesetz (BMG) § 6 Accuracy and Completeness of the Register, Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection ↩

  4. Bundesmeldegesetz (BMG) § 12 Right to Correction, Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection ↩

entry.title: Markthalle Neun
entry.content:
IX

This is one of the 14 market halls built in Berlin during the 1800s. While many were destroyed during the war or neglected over time as they fell behind the trends, some have been reconstructed through community-led efforts.

Aside from DM, you won’t find any major corporate franchises at Markthalle Neun. Despite that—or perhaps because of it—the place is packed with locals, travelers, and Kreuzberg hipsters every Street Food Thursday and Saturday afternoon.

In this post, I’ll share a few spots I visit often.

Food Stalls

DM

This is where I buy my water.

Frisch Gefischt

You can get sushi-grade fish here that’s safe to eat raw. They also serve fish and chips, which is good enough to be worth a dedicated trip. Just a heads-up: it occasionally disappears from the menu.

Big Stuff Smoked BBQ

The pulled pork seems to be the popular choice, but I personally prefer the pork belly or beef brisket. You can have it served platter-style on a tray, or as a sandwich—their brioche buns are excellent.

Sironi

I usually go here for pizza or focaccia. I’m a big fan of the mortadella.

Zoom Fresh

A kimchi shop run by a Korean owner. You can grab a bowl of Janchi-guksu (warm noodle soup) for under 10 EUR.

Restaurant

Marktlokal

The mushroom dish pictured above was absolutely delicious. It can be a bit tough to get a reservation sometimes.

Photos ©️ Markthalle Neun website

entry.title: Student Residence Permit in Germany
entry.content:
I finally received my student residence permit1. I had been preparing for it even before admission, but I was only able to wrap up the whole process after finishing my first semester. I’m leaving this short note here to record my trial and error, along with some new things I learned and felt throughout this exhausting journey.

Visum vs. Aufenthaltserlaubnis

According to the Embassy of the Federal Republic of Germany in Seoul, “If you plan to stay for more than 90 days or if your purpose of stay is not tourism or a business trip, you must apply for a visa.”2 However, thanks to the visa agreement between South Korea and Germany (effective Jan 1, 2005), Korean nationals can “also apply for visa issuance at the local immigration office within 90 days of entering Germany.”3 That being said, local immigration offices in Germany issue a residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis) rather than a visa (Visum), so the document you get locally seems to mean a residence permit. In my case, I already had a visa issued by the German Embassy in Seoul before entering the country for the first time, and I needed to change my residence status for my studies.

Berlin

Online Application (2025-09-29)

You can fill out the application form and upload all the necessary documents right on the Landesamt für Einwanderung (Berlin Immigration Office) website. No need to print out papers and carry them around in a binder! The submitted documents were as follows:4

  1. Application form (Auto-generated after filling out the online form)
  2. Proof of health insurance
  3. Passport
  4. Currently valid visa or residence permit
  5. Registration of address (Anmeldung)
  6. Blocked account (Sperrkonto)
    1. Account opening confirmation
    2. Bank balance certificate
  7. Letter of admission (Zulassungsbescheid)

At the final step, I paid the 100-euro fee by card. I was quite amazed that this entire process was possible without an appointment (Termin), paper documents, or cash.

Fiktionsbescheinigung (2025-10-8)

Just two days later, I received an email from the Berlin Immigration Office with a scheduled date and time for my visit. It included instructions to come and pick up a temporary residence permit. On the spot, they checked my passport and visa, I paid the 13-euro issuance fee (card only), and I received it right away. The duration was a generous 6 months, giving me plenty of time to go through the next steps.

Although there isn’t much you can actually do with it, a temporary residence permit (Fiktionsbescheinigung) inherits the exact conditions of your existing visa or residence permit. If you originally entered visa-free for 90 days and fail to get your desired residence permit quickly, you might face work restrictions or, more importantly, a situation where you leave Germany (outside the German border, not just the EU!) and cannot re-enter. You need to check if you fall under the condition of Der Aufenthaltstitel als fortbestehend (§ 81 Abs. 4 AufenthG).

Just to be sure, I asked the clerk about the status of my student residence permit application and got an unexpected answer: the process had been paused. Before I asked, absolutely no one had formally notified me of this crucial fact (and still hasn’t..). The reason was that the Berlin Immigration Office can only issue student residence permits to students residing within Berlin and Brandenburg. They told me there was no need to cancel the application itself; once I registered my address in Aachen, my case would automatically be transferred to the local immigration office there, and I could just pick up where I left off. Since I hadn’t even found an apartment in Aachen yet and my temporary permit still had plenty of time left, I decided to just forget about this whole process for a while.

Aachen

Immigration Office Registration

I finally signed a housing contract and swiftly completed my address registration (Anmeldung) on the very same day. But when I tried to book an appointment with the Aachen Immigration Office, it didn’t work. I went to the office one morning when I had some free time, waited in line, and was told that I had to register my information into their system first. This was a step that didn’t exist in Berlin. Fortunately, I brought my passport, residence permit, and Anmeldung, so I applied for registration right there. However, it takes 1-2 weeks for the registration to go through, during which you can’t do anything at all, not even book an appointment.

Booking an Appointment (2025-12-11)

They didn’t send any separate notification regarding the registration result. I just checked the website one day, saw that the system allowed me to book an appointment, and scheduled it for an available day. Of course, the earliest available date was 2 months later…

Student Residence Permit Application (2026-02-25)

I finally finished applying for the student residence permit. Honestly, after dealing with the aforementioned trial and error, side tasks, and waiting for the appointment, I was only just beginning the very first step toward acquiring the actual permit. Nevertheless, perhaps because there was a record of my application being submitted in Berlin and transferred over to Aachen, I was able to get an interim certificate approving my residence permit right on the spot (Vorläufige Bescheinigung gem. § 3 7 Abs.2 VwVfG NRW über einen bewilligten Aufenthaltstitel).

On this day, I printed out and brought all the previously submitted documents along with some updated ones.

  1. Application form (Aachen Immigration Office PDF form5)
  2. Proof of health insurance
  3. Passport (I had my passport reissued in the meantime…)
    1. Expired passport
    2. Currently valid passport
  4. Currently valid visa or residence permit
    1. Previous visa
    2. Temporary residence permit (Fiktionsbescheinigung)
  5. Registration of address (Anmeldung)
  6. Blocked account (Sperrkonto)
    1. Account opening confirmation
    2. Bank balance certificate (most recent issue date)
  7. Certificate of enrollment
    1. Certificate of study (Immatrikulationsbescheinigung)
  8. Passport photo

I didn’t have to pay the application fee since I had already paid it in Berlin.

Since I got a new passport, I was worried about my passport details being different from my initial application. I even went out of my way to prepare my passport issuance history in English from Government24 with an online Apostille certificate, but they handled it with just a simple visual check.

The rule for passport photos had changed; you must now submit photos taken either at the on-site kiosk or at a photo studio that provides a QR code. The notice I read said to bring a biometric photo, so I was caught off guard and unintentionally ended up getting my picture taken on the spot looking like a mugshot…

You can check the issuance status online, and a little less than 2 weeks later, the status changed to ready for pickup. The clerk had told me it usually takes 2 to 4 weeks. You can apply for an express service for an additional fee. From what I heard from people around me, they managed to get it in 5 days with that option.

Picking up the Student Residence Permit (2026-04-13)

Even picking it up requires an appointment… I thought it was all over, but the final hurdle was waiting. The next available date popped up as 3 weeks away. I spent a few days refreshing the page whenever I thought about it, and luckily, an early morning slot on a closer date opened up, so I managed to squeeze it into my schedule.

I thought I would just be picking it up, but it took some time because I had to sit down with a staff member at the desk for identity verification and the cancellation of my old residence permit.

Then I came home, set up my BundID, and finally, this whole process was over.

Banner image ©️ RWTH Aachen

  2. Original text from the website of the Embassy of the Federal Republic of Germany in Seoul (Korean) ↩

  3. Original text from the website of the Embassy of the Federal Republic of Germany in Seoul (Korean) ↩
